slice: Debt wobbles. Hype soars. France strains. Bugs bite. IT trims. Scrap pays. Smell travels.

callouts.text: Anthropic Q3 revenue, up 45% on Q2, as its IPO nears (ET)
Anthropic's annual run rate (ARR), a metric Damodaran says needs care

stories.title: CoreWeave's debt pile tests whether the AI build-out can be financed
points: CoreWeave, an AI cloud firm built on borrowed money, has become a test of whether the AI build-out can be financed. Investors have been selling its shares and bonds.

Its model: sign a contract with a big customer such as Microsoft, then borrow against it, with chips as collateral. Other borrowing is repaid from corporate cash, so debt sits on top of debt; the total is $35.4 billion.
Rising Treasury yields and hot inflation raised borrowing costs, and yields on its existing debt passed 15%. One startup CEO says Goldman bankers could not explain the slide.
numbers: yield on its debt at the peak
stories.why: AI's story is shifting from technology to financing. If credit gets dearer, neoclouds may have to sell shares, and big-customer contracts become the real collateral.
stories.other: CoreWeave's CEO calls it a market misunderstanding, Nvidia's Jensen Huang voices confidence, and Goldman's analysts upgraded the stock. Project loans are repaid from customer contracts, so a falling share price is not the same as default.
stories.imageAlt: Graphic: CoreWeave owes $35.4 billion; it borrows against customer contracts, and yields on its debt topped 15% as borrowing costs rose.
stories.emailTeaser: The AI build-out's financing is under test.
stories.cite: CoreWeave owes $35.4 billion as of 30 June 2026, The Information reports (15 October 2026).

stories.title: SpaceX-Tesla merger and Anthropic IPO: how investors price AI
points: The FT's Big Read says Elon Musk wants SpaceX and Tesla combined into one AI-led company worth about $3.5tn, with pay awards that could reach $1.7tn.
Anthropic told investors its third-quarter revenue was $16.8bn, up 45% on the quarter, and profitable on an adjusted basis, with an annual run rate of $67bn, Damodaran notes.
Damodaran says young, loss-making firms are priced on buzzy metrics, from eyeballs to users to ARR, and warns that ARR can be defined in different ways.
stories.why: Whether it is a mega-merger or an IPO, investors are paying for a story. Metrics like ARR, and pay targets tied to market value, shape how big that story looks.
stories.other: Bulls say AI's market is vast and the leaders will take most of it. Bears say compute costs, cheaper open-source rivals and rules could squeeze margins, and critics see the merger as a way to shift attention from a weaker Tesla. Damodaran takes no side until the full prospectus is filed.

also.title: Damodaran: From Eyeballs to Annual Run Rates

stories.imageAlt: Explainer: Musk's proposed SpaceX-Tesla union and Anthropic's IPO are priced on stories; Anthropic's $67bn annual run rate sits against $16.8bn of Q3 revenue, and ARR definitions vary.
stories.src: Financial Times, The Economic Times and Musings on Markets
stories.emailTeaser: Musk's merger and Anthropic's IPO ask what a story is worth.
stories.cite: Anthropic reported third-quarter revenue of $16.8bn, up 45% from the second quarter, Aswath Damodaran wrote on 22 Oct 2026.

stories.title: TCS and Infosys: AI tops 10% of revenue, yet pricing bites
points: TCS and Infosys both say AI brought in more than 10% of revenue in Q2 FY27, and most of India's top five IT firms widened operating margins.
Clients want the savings passed on. Infosys cut its FY27 growth guidance to 1-2% in constant currency, from 1.5-3%, and says it will favour profitable deals over growth.
CEO Salil Parekh sees a big cyber opening as AI models uncover flaws, and says Infosys is already sharing defences with clients, though budgets may not rise much.
numbers: Infosys AI share of Q2 revenue
stories.why: There is no standard way to count AI revenue, so firms are hard to compare. The test is how much of the productivity gain they keep as clients negotiate.
stories.other: Less effort need not mean less profit, as HFS Research's Phil Fersht argues, if firms price on outcomes. And clients may fund cyber work by trimming elsewhere.
stories.imageAlt: Graphic: AI was 10.5% of Infosys's Q2 revenue (about $539 million) and TCS's annualised AI revenue is $3.1 billion, while Infosys cut its FY27 growth guidance to 1-2%.
stories.emailTeaser: AI crosses 10% of revenue as clients demand savings back.
stories.cite: Infosys said AI was 10.5% of its Q2 FY27 revenue, about $539 million, up 29% sequentially (Moneycontrol, 24 October 2026).

stories.title: France's riots meet a debt squeeze, and youth want the system fixed
points: The WSJ says years of subsidies to cushion prices have left France with one of Europe's biggest deficits, and investors have pushed its 10-year borrowing costs above 5%.
It adds that stagnant real incomes, a heavy tax burden and pension costs hidden in ministry budgets leave little room for new help.

The FT's Simon Kuper describes looting in Paris and polls that put Marine Le Pen in line to win next year's election, while a Janan Ganesh column argues the young protesters mostly want a fairer system, not a new one.
stories.why: Protests need money to answer them, and markets are now charging France more to borrow it. That narrows the choices for whoever wins next year.
stories.other: Kuper notes the French often talk radical but act conservative, and Ganesh reads the protests as a bid to make the existing system work. So the anger may be answerable through budget choices, but the bond market may not wait for them.

also.title: FT column: The young are conformists in denial

stories.imageAlt: Explainer: French 10-year borrowing costs above 5% squeeze a state facing riots; stalled incomes and hidden pension costs limit help, and polls put Marine Le Pen ahead.
stories.src: The Wall Street Journal and Financial Times
stories.emailTeaser: Riots, pricey debt and students who want in, not out.

stories.title: AI finds bugs faster and attackers follow in 'Black October'
points: The WSJ reports a wave of attacks using AI agents and hacking tools, adopted by China- and Russia-linked groups and ordinary criminals.

Reuters spoke to seven cybersecurity professionals who say AI-found flaws will almost certainly cause more outages like this week's PHP-related ones on government sites. VulnCheck says flaws found doubled year on year, with AI a driver.
Models can scan code round the clock and turn exploits around in hours. Experts split on whether attackers gain: curl's lead developer says AI-found bugs tend to be exotic.
numbers: of websites exposed to new bugs (WSJ)
stories.why: Attackers use AI to move faster than people can respond, and patch windows shrink from weeks to hours. Patching speed becomes a core security measure.
stories.other: More disclosed flaws do not automatically mean more successful attacks, and AI also helps defenders. A Hunt.io researcher said the criminals he tracked had not yet built a working PHP exploit by Thursday afternoon.
stories.imageAlt: Graphic: digital flaws found doubled year on year per VulnCheck, AI can turn exploits around in hours, and new web bugs exposed many sites.
stories.src: The Wall Street Journal and Reuters
stories.emailTeaser: Experts expect more fire drills as AI finds flaws faster.
stories.cite: AI helped drive a doubling of digital flaws found year on year, says VulnCheck research due out soon (Reuters, 23 October 2026).

stories.title: US recyclers harvest rare earths from old wind turbines
points: The WSJ says Paladin EnviroTech is pulling rare-earth magnets from retired wind turbines in Iowa, hoping to cut US reliance on China.
Only a fraction of older turbines carry rare earths, but newer, more powerful ones hold much more, so supply grows as fleets are replaced.
Dismantling huge parts and separating the metals cheaply are the hard parts; most recyclers so far chased copper instead.
numbers: of replaced Highland turbines hold rare earths (WSJ)
stories.why: Recycling is a faster, smaller route than new mines to ease dependence on China for the magnets in motors, drones and scanners, if the economics work.
stories.other: Few turbines carry rare earths, and battery-recycling ventures have stumbled before on supply and cost. This can complement new mines, not replace them.
stories.imageAlt: Explainer: retired wind-turbine generators hold rare-earth magnets; about 20% of replaced Highland turbines have them and Paladin has roughly 500 lined up.
stories.emailTeaser: Paladin targets turbine magnets to loosen China's grip.

stories.title: 'Scentronic' prototype senses a smell and recreates it far away
points: Ohio State researchers built an e-nose that spots a smell, then tells a small remote device to release a matching scent, at any distance.
It knows five scents so far: beer, cake, coffee, oranges and red wine. Scent molecules do not travel online; only the odour data does.
It is a research prototype built without a company. Mixed smells, refills, cost and safety of the mist are open questions.
stories.why: Sight and sound already travel digitally; smell is the gap. A real product would need many more scents and reliable sensing of mixtures.
stories.other: Recognising a smell and recreating it are separate challenges, the lead author says. Five scents is a demo, not a library.
stories.imageAlt: Graphic: the Scentronic e-nose recognises five scents (beer, cake, coffee, oranges, red wine) and a remote device recreates them.
stories.emailTeaser: A lab prototype senses five scents and recreates them remotely.
stories.cite: Researchers say the Scentronic e-nose recognises five scents so far, in a Science Advances study (Reuters, 23 October 2026).

takeaway.line: Metrics flatter young firms and developed economies alike: the headline number arrives first, the cost second. Ask who pays, and when, before you trust it.
